claims.text: The starting material is a single-phase, titanium-rich high-entropy alloy containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each.
The heavy-transition-metal fraction can be varied while retaining a single-phase solid solution.
Increasing the proportion of heavy transition metals such as Hf or Zr enhances lattice distortion.
Increasing heavy-transition-metal content modifies local atomic arrangements.
Enhanced lattice distortion and modified local arrangements alter the phonon density of states and shift vibrational modes.
The phonon-spectrum changes caused by added heavy transition metals enhance electron-phonon coupling.
Electron-phonon interactions contribute to superconducting pairing in titanium-containing refractory high-entropy alloys.
Enhanced electron-phonon coupling increases superconducting pairing probability and raises Tc.
Increasing Hf or Zr content will raise Tc relative to the baseline titanium-rich alloy.
Tc will correlate systematically with the degree of heavy-metal incorporation.
The proposed behavior applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution without secondary-phase formation.
Excessive compositional modification may produce structural instability, phase separation, or secondary phases.
Disorder effects may compete with the proposed enhancement of electron-phonon coupling.
A lack of measurable Tc change across the composition series would falsify the hypothesis.
A decrease in electron-phonon-coupling indicators as heavy-metal content increases would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The heavy-transition-metal fraction cannot be increased while simultaneously keeping the overall stoichiometry or all element ratios constant; a compensating compositional change must be specified.
The hypothesis and mechanism predict a directional increase in Tc, whereas the predicted outcome permits merely systematic modulation, which could include no increase or a decrease.

Phase separation is excluded by the stated applicability boundary but is also classified as a falsifying result. Phase separation would instead move the experiment outside the hypothesis's stated domain unless the hypothesis explicitly predicts phase stability.
